title: How to Choose a Fulfillment Partner for Art Prints and Wall Decor
excerpt: Art prints and wall decor stress fulfillment in ways apparel never does: dimensional shipping, framing quality, and damage rates. A four-factor selection framework.
body: Selling art prints and wall decor online is a fulfillment problem wearing an art problem's clothes. The product is fragile, often oversized, frequently needs framing, and its value is entirely in condition on arrival. A print that arrives creased is a full loss plus a refund, so the fulfillment partner decision matters more here than in almost any other category. Four factors separate the partners that can handle this category from the ones that merely list it in their catalog.

Factor one is dimensional shipping competence. Large prints and framed pieces hit dimensional weight pricing, which means shipping costs jump non-linearly with size, and a platform whose flat shipping rates were designed for t-shirts will either lose you money on every large order or force prices nobody pays. Ask specifically how the partner calculates rates for oversized and framed items, whether tubes versus flat packaging are options per product, and what the actual shipped cost is for your three largest SKUs, not the smallest.

Factor two is framing and finishing quality. If your catalog includes framed prints, canvas wraps, or poster hangers, request samples of each construction type. Check corner joints on frames, canvas tension, glass versus acrylic choices, and how the hanging hardware ships. Production networks like Gooten's route these SKUs to specialized facilities, which is why quality can differ sharply between product lines on the same platform; the DTCwise tool page at /tool/gooten maps its decor production categories in detail.

Factor three is damage rate and the response to it. Ask the direct question: what percentage of framed items arrive damaged, and what happens then? Good partners track this number and reprint without argument. Bad partners treat each damage claim as an exception requiring debate. Also check packaging construction for large formats: corner protectors, rigid mailers, and tube choices are cheap for the partner and decisive for you.

Factor four is catalog integration for variants. Art stores live on size variants, orientation options, and frame choices, and each variant multiplies SKUs. Confirm the platform's product builder handles variant-level pricing and mockups without manual duplication, because a catalog of two hundred prints times five sizes becomes unmanageable if every variant is a separate product entry. Test this during the trial, not after migration.

The DTCwise Fulfillment and Shipping category at /category/fulfillment compares partners on oversized-item handling and per-category fit, including which networks treat art prints as a specialty rather than an afterthought. Sample your largest, most fragile SKU with the finalist before migrating the catalog, and let the condition on arrival make the decision.
